article.title: GitHub Ships Enterprise MCP Server Allowlists for Copilot, Enforced Fail-Closed Across App, CLI, and VS Code
article.summary: GitHub made allowedMcpServers and deniedMcpServers keys generally available, letting enterprises centrally block MCP servers Copilot clients can run.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

GitHub has made general availability of a new pair of enterprise managed-settings keys, `allowedMcpServers` and `deniedMcpServers`, that let enterprise owners centrally control which Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers GitHub Copilot clients are permitted to run, according to [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-08-06-mcp-allowlists-in-enterprise-managed-settings/). The change, published August 6, 2026, extends the governance controls enterprises already have over Copilot into the growing set of external MCP servers that agentic coding sessions can connect to for extra tools and data sources.

## What We Know

- The two new keys go into `copilot/managed-settings.json`, and each is "a list of matchers that identify MCP servers by remote URL, local command, or name," per [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-08-06-mcp-allowlists-in-enterprise-managed-settings/).
- Three matcher types are supported: `serverUrl`, which "matches remote (HTTP/SSE) servers" and "supports `*` wildcards and canonicalizes URLs to prevent evasion"; `serverCommand`, which "matches local (stdio) servers by exact command and arguments"; and `serverName`, which "matches the user-assigned label" but is, in GitHub's own words, "only supplied as a convenience, not a security control, since users can rename servers," according to [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-08-06-mcp-allowlists-in-enterprise-managed-settings/).
- The policy is enforced fail-closed: GitHub states that policies "fail closed, meaning a malformed or unverifiable configuration is blocked rather than allowed," and when settings are layered, "a server must pass every layer," per [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-08-06-mcp-allowlists-in-enterprise-managed-settings/).
- Both keys can be marked `overridable` in server-managed deployments, which GitHub says lets "enterprise teams define their own allow and deny lists on top of your baseline," per [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-08-06-mcp-allowlists-in-enterprise-managed-settings/).
- Enforcement currently covers three surfaces: "the GitHub Copilot app, Copilot CLI and VS Code," according to [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-08-06-mcp-allowlists-in-enterprise-managed-settings/).
- To turn it on, administrators add the keys to `copilot/managed-settings.json` inside their source organization's `.github-private` repository and commit to the default branch, per [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-08-06-mcp-allowlists-in-enterprise-managed-settings/) and [GitHub Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/administer-copilot/manage-mcp-usage/configure-enterprise-allowlist), which adds that the file "you can also install it directly on users' machines using mobile device management."
- GitHub's documentation lays out the exact order clients evaluate a server against the policy: built-in default servers such as the GitHub MCP server are always allowed first; the server is then blocked if it matches any `deniedMcpServers` entry; if `allowedMcpServers` is present, the server is blocked unless it matches an entry there; and finally, the server is blocked if its URL or command contains "an unresolved variable, such as `${VARIABLE}` or `$VARIABLE`, because the client cannot verify the server," according to [GitHub Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/administer-copilot/manage-mcp-usage/configure-enterprise-allowlist).
- The documentation's own example configuration allows a Playwright MCP server (`npx @playwright/mcp@latest`) and a Markdown-conversion server (`markitdown-mcp`) while explicitly denying a filesystem server configured with root access, noting that "the filesystem server configured to access the root filesystem is always blocked, even if it also matches an allowlist entry," per [GitHub Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/administer-copilot/manage-mcp-usage/configure-enterprise-allowlist).
- If the policy file itself is broken, GitHub says the client falls back to the safest interpretation: "If an allowlist or denylist is malformed (for example, has invalid JSON), the client treats the policy as an empty `allowedMcpServers` list. This blocks all servers except built-in default servers," per [GitHub Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/administer-copilot/manage-mcp-usage/configure-enterprise-allowlist).
- The same fail-safe logic applies when a client can't even retrieve its policy: it "retains the previously enforced policy," and "the effective policy can become more restrictive, but not less restrictive," according to [GitHub Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/administer-copilot/manage-mcp-usage/configure-enterprise-allowlist).
- The feature is scoped to enterprise owners on Copilot Enterprise or Copilot Business plans, per [GitHub Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/administer-copilot/manage-mcp-usage/configure-enterprise-allowlist).

## What We Don't Know

GitHub's changelog post does not disclose adoption numbers, whether any customer requested the feature, or whether it followed a specific security incident. Neither source describes enforcement timelines for clients beyond the three currently listed, and GitHub has not said whether support for additional Copilot surfaces, such as its JetBrains or Xcode integrations, is planned.

## Why It Matters

MCP has become the standard way Copilot's agentic modes reach outside a codebase to internal APIs, databases, and other tools, which also makes an unvetted MCP server a potential path for credential theft or data exfiltration if a developer connects to a malicious or misconfigured one. By moving allowlist enforcement into the same `managed-settings.json` file enterprises already use for other Copilot governance, and by defaulting to a deny-first, fail-closed posture when a policy can't be verified, GitHub is treating MCP server trust as a baseline enterprise control rather than an opt-in setting left to individual developers.
